title: How to build a nut gift box people will use
description: Plan a nut gift box with a good mix of flavours, textures and sizes. Ideas for themes, packing tips, and when to buy a ready-made box instead.
html:
A good nut gift box is easy to like and easy to use. It does not need ribbons the size of a dinner plate. It needs a thoughtful mix, a sensible size, and a few things the recipient can eat now and a few they can keep. Here is how to plan one, whether you are filling a tin for a colleague or a hamper for the whole family.

Start with the person

Before choosing a single nut, think about who it is for.

  • The snacker wants roasted, salted and flavoured nuts they can open and eat.
  • The baker wants ingredients: ground almonds, chopped walnuts, pecan pieces.
  • The toast-and-spread fan wants jars and butters.
  • The host wants something that looks good on a table and can be shared.

If you are not sure, aim for a mix of snackable and cookable. It is hard to get that wrong.

Aim for contrast

A box that is all one texture or flavour gets dull quickly. Include variety:

  • Something crunchy and roasted, such as dry-roasted almonds or salted cashews.
  • Something sweet, like maple-glazed pecans or honey-roasted peanuts.
  • Something with a kick, like a chilli or smoked flavour.
  • Something rich and spreadable, such as a jar of nut butter.
  • Something plain, for those who prefer simple flavours or want to cook.

Our post on building a trail mix takes the same approach on a smaller scale: balance sweet, salty, crunchy and chewy, and you rarely go wrong.

Choose a theme

Themes make a box feel intentional.

The tasting box

Several small portions of different nuts, so the recipient can compare. Almonds, cashews, hazelnuts and pecans, each in a separate bag, plus a card saying which is which. It is a natural fit for curious eaters.

The baker's box

Raw and chopped nuts, some flour-style ingredients, a recipe card. You could include a handwritten copy of a favourite, such as our walnut banana bread.

The breakfast box

A jar of granola or crunch mix, a pot of nut butter, a few single-serve bags of nuts for the desk. Easy to use, and it feels like a treat.

The festive box

Spiced, glazed and sweet nuts, plus something rich and chocolatey. This is the one where it is fine to go a little extravagant.

Think about size and packing

  • Small and neat suits a tin, a jar or a small box with a few items.
  • Medium suits a shallow tray with four to six items.
  • Large is for a hamper with jars, bags and perhaps a bowl or board.

Pack heavy jars on the bottom and lighter bags on top. Keep sweet and savoury items in their own bags so flavours do not mix. Fill any gaps with paper or a folded cloth so nothing rattles. If you are posting it, add a layer of padding, and check the shipping and returns page for timing so it arrives fresh.

Keep freshness in mind

Nuts stay best when they are cool, dry and sealed. Avoid packing them next to anything that gives off heat or moisture. Our post on storing nuts so they stay fresh has more tips you can pass on to the recipient. A small card with a "best enjoyed within" note is a thoughtful touch.

A note on allergies

Always think about who will open the box. If you do not know a person's allergies, ask, or choose something other than nuts. If you are gifting to a household with allergy concerns, include labels or a list of contents, and tell them what is inside. Read the label on every product. For anything medical, a qualified professional is the right person to ask. The FSA allergy guidance and FDA food allergy page are useful general references.

Or buy one ready-made

If you would rather skip the assembling, the gift boxes category has options. The small gift box suits a thank-you, the big nut hamper is a crowd-pleaser, and the nut butter trio is ideal for anyone who lives on toast.

The finishing touch

Add a short handwritten note and a suggestion of how to enjoy it. A gift is never really about the nuts. They are just a very tasty way of saying you thought of someone.

title: Are peanuts really nuts? A plain explainer
description: Peanuts grow underground and belong to the legume family, yet they are treated as nuts in the kitchen. Here is how botany and cooking differ.
html:
Ask a botanist and a cook whether a peanut is a nut, and you may get two different answers. Both are right. The disagreement comes from the fact that "nut" means one thing in a plant science lecture and something quite different at the supermarket. Here is the short, friendly guide.

What the botanist says

In botany, a true nut is a hard-shelled fruit that does not split open to release its seed. Chestnuts and hazelnuts fit that description. So do acorns.

Peanuts do not. The peanut plant is a legume, in the same family as peas, beans and lentils. The peanut shell is a pod, and that pod holds seeds, much like a pea pod does. The botanical story is covered on the peanut page on Wikipedia.

So by the strict plant definition, a peanut is a legume, not a nut.

How peanuts grow

Peanuts have a curious habit. The plant flowers above ground, then the flower stalk bends down, pushes into the soil, and the pod develops underground. That is why peanuts are sometimes called groundnuts.

Pea pods grow in the air, and peanut pods grow in the soil. It is one of the more unusual things in the plant world, and the reason peanuts are harvested by digging up the plant.

What the cook says

In the kitchen, a nut is any dry, crunchy, oil-rich kernel that you can eat on its own, roast, grind or bake with. That includes almonds, cashews, walnuts and pecans. It also includes peanuts, which behave just like them.

Peanuts are roasted, salted, ground into butter, scattered over salads and crushed into sauces, exactly as other nuts are. For anyone shopping, cooking or snacking, a peanut is a nut in every way that counts.

Not every "nut" is a nut

If you start looking, the list of exceptions is long:

  • Almonds are seeds of a stone fruit, related to peaches.
  • Cashews are seeds that hang from the outside of a fruit stalk. (We cover the oddities in where cashews come from.)
  • Pistachios and pine nuts are also seeds.
  • Brazil nuts are seeds from a large pod.

The food world uses "nut" as a loose, practical word for a whole group of similar-looking foods. Botanists use it for a narrow category. Both usages are fine, as long as you know which one is being used.

Why this matters for allergies

This is where the distinction is more than trivia. Peanut allergy and tree nut allergy are separate things. Peanuts are legumes, while tree nuts such as walnuts, almonds and cashews come from trees. Allergy labels and advice often treat the two groups separately, and some people are allergic to one group but not the other. You can read general background on peanut allergy and on tree nut allergy.

Because peanuts and tree nuts are often handled in the same places, labels commonly mention both. Our guide to reading food labels for nut allergies explains what to look for. This is general information only, not medical advice. Always read the label, and ask a qualified professional about any medical question.

Peanuts in the kitchen

Peanuts are among the most versatile nuts you can cook with.

  • Snack on honey-roasted peanuts for a sweet-and-salty crunch.
  • Spread smooth peanut butter on toast, or reach for crunchy peanut butter if you like texture.
  • Roast raw peanuts yourself at about 160C (325F) for 15 to 20 minutes, until they smell warm and nutty.
  • Grind them for satay-style sauces, or crush them over noodles.

Making your own spread is simple, and our post on homemade nut butter works for peanuts as well as almonds.

So, are they nuts?

Botanically, no. In the kitchen, yes. Pick whichever answer suits the conversation. At a dinner table, "yes" is the friendlier option. In a botany class, you will want to say "legume" and look quietly pleased with yourself.

title: Why nuts go rancid
description: Learn why nuts turn rancid, from oxidation of natural oils to heat and light, and how to spot the smell, taste and look of stale nuts.
html:
Everyone has bitten into a stale nut and regretted it. The taste is sharp, a bit soapy, sometimes like old paint or a forgotten crayon. It spoils a snack, ruins a cake and makes you wonder how a bag that smelled so good last month could turn so quickly. The explanation is chemistry, and once you know it, the storage rules make perfect sense.

What rancid actually means

Rancid describes fats and oils that have broken down and developed unpleasant flavours and smells. Nuts are rich in natural oils, which gives them their creamy texture and rich taste. Those same oils are what make them vulnerable.

Rancidification is the general name for the process. It does not mean a nut has been contaminated. It means the nut's own fat has changed.

The main cause: oxidation

Most rancidity in nuts comes from oxidation. Oxygen in the air reacts with the unsaturated fats in the oil, breaking them into smaller molecules. Some of those molecules are volatile and smell strong, which is what you notice as the off aroma.

Oxidation happens slowly in a sealed, cool, dark space, and faster in warm, bright, airy ones. Several things speed it up:

  • Heat. Warm temperatures increase the rate of nearly every chemical reaction, including this one.
  • Light. Sunlight and strong indoor light give energy to the reactions.
  • Air. More oxygen means more oxidation. An opened bag is exposed to fresh air every time.
  • Exposed surfaces. A nut with a broken surface has more oil in contact with air than a whole one.

Not all nuts are equal

Nuts differ in the kind of fat they hold, and that affects how quickly they turn.

  • Walnuts, pecans and pine nuts contain higher levels of polyunsaturated fats, which oxidise more readily. They are among the quickest to go stale. See raw walnut halves, raw pecan halves and pine nuts for some examples.
  • Almonds, hazelnuts and cashews are somewhat more stable, though they still change over time.
  • Brazil nuts are very rich in oil, so raw Brazil nuts benefit from cool, sealed storage like the others.

This is a general pattern rather than a precise ranking. Variety, handling and storage conditions all play a role, so use your senses rather than assuming a date on the packet is the whole story.

Why chopped, ground and roasted nuts go faster

Surface area matters. A whole nut has a protective shell, or at least an intact skin, that limits how much oil meets the air. Chop it and you expose more. Grind it into powder and you expose a great deal more.

Roasting adds heat, which changes the structure of the nut and can drive some oils toward the surface. Roasted nuts often taste wonderful at first and fade faster. That is why a jar of roasted almonds is usually best eaten within a few weeks, while raw whole ones may last much longer. The differences are covered in raw vs roasted nuts.

How to spot rancid nuts

Your senses are the best test.

  1. Smell first. Fresh nuts smell sweet, nutty or neutral. Rancid ones smell sharp, sour, bitter, soapy, or like paint, putty or old oil.
  2. Then taste one. A harsh, bitter or metallic taste is the giveaway. If it tastes wrong, stop eating and discard the batch.
  3. Look at texture. Rancid nuts can feel slightly oily, sticky or limp, though soft nuts are not always rancid.
  4. Check for mould. This is a different problem entirely. Any visible mould, dark patches or a damp, musty smell means the nuts should go in the bin.

Do not rely on appearance alone. Nuts can look perfectly fine and still taste off. And be cautious about eating nuts you suspect have turned. They may not be dangerous in small amounts, but the flavour is awful, and when in doubt, throw them out. If you have concerns about food safety, a qualified professional can advise you.

Keeping rancidity at bay

You cannot stop oxidation completely, but you can slow it dramatically.

  • Keep them cool. A cool cupboard is good. The fridge is better. The freezer is best for long storage.
  • Keep them dark. Use opaque containers, or store clear jars in a closed cupboard.
  • Keep them sealed. Airtight containers, freezer bags with the air pressed out, or vacuum-sealed pouches all help.
  • Buy small. Especially for oily nuts you only use occasionally.
  • Label and rotate. Write the date on the container and use the oldest first.
  • Buy whole when you can. Chop or grind just before use.

Our full guide to this topic is storing nuts so they stay fresh, including how to bring nuts out of cold storage without making them soggy.

Can you rescue slightly stale nuts?

If nuts are merely soft, not rancid, a few minutes in a warm oven at 150C (300F) will crisp them up. But heat cannot fix a rancid flavour. Once the oils have turned, the taste is baked in, and toasting just makes it more obvious. If a nut smells or tastes wrong, it is past saving.

A last word

Rancidity is not a mystery or a sign that something went wrong at the shop. It is a natural result of what nuts are made of: tasty, oily and sensitive to air. Cool, dark and sealed will keep most nuts tasting the way they should. And if you sniff a jar and the smell makes you wince, trust your nose and start fresh.

title: Storing nuts so they stay fresh
description: Keep nuts crisp and sweet-tasting with simple storage rules (cool, dark, airtight), plus when to use the fridge or freezer and how to check freshness.
html:
A bag of nuts left on the counter for a month tells a sad story. The crunch softens, the sweetness fades, and the taste drifts toward something flat and faintly paint-like. The cause is not mysterious. Nuts are rich in natural oils, and oils react with air, light and warmth. The fix is not complicated either: keep them cool, dark and sealed, and buy only what you will use in a reasonable time.

The three enemies

Heat. Warmth speeds up the chemical changes that make oils turn stale. A cupboard next to the oven is the worst possible spot.

Light. Sunlight and bright kitchen lights also help break down fats. Clear jars on a sunny windowsill look lovely and keep nuts badly.

Air and moisture. Oxygen drives staleness, and damp air makes nuts soft or even mouldy. Leaving a bag open invites both.

If you remember nothing else, remember this trio. Everything below is a way of keeping nuts away from them.

Pantry storage

For nuts you will eat within a few weeks, the cupboard is fine if it is truly cool and dark.

  1. Move nuts from their original bag into an airtight container, such as a glass jar with a rubber seal or a tin with a snug lid.
  2. Choose a container that fits the quantity. A half-empty jar holds extra air.
  3. Store it away from the cooker, kettle and sunny windows.
  4. Label the lid with the purchase date. Memory is unreliable.

Whole, shelled raw nuts such as raw almonds are the most stable in a pantry. Roasted nuts, ground nuts and chopped nuts have more exposed surface, so they do not keep as long.

Fridge and freezer

Cold slows the reactions that spoil nuts, which makes the fridge and freezer excellent for anything you will not use quickly.

  • Fridge: good for a few months, especially for nuts with a higher oil content such as walnut halves and pecan halves. Keep them in a sealed container so they do not pick up odours from other foods.
  • Freezer: suitable for longer storage. Use freezer bags with the air squeezed out, or a rigid container, and label them with the date.

When you take nuts out of cold storage, let the sealed container come to room temperature before opening it. Opening it early lets condensation form on the nuts, which makes them soggy. Most nuts also freeze without clumping, so you can scoop out just what you need and reseal.

If you want a quick crispness boost after cold storage, warm them on a tray at 150C (300F) for 5 minutes and cool again.

Which nuts need extra care

Not all nuts keep equally well.

  • Walnuts and pecans: high in oils, so they benefit most from the fridge or freezer.
  • Almonds and hazelnuts: fairly sturdy when whole, but ground or flaked forms go stale sooner.
  • Cashews: moderate keepers, best in a cool, sealed container.
  • Pine nuts: very oily and quick to turn, so buy small amounts and store cold. Our pine nuts are best used soon after opening.
  • Chopped and ground nuts: more surface area means faster staleness. Store them cold and use within a few weeks.

For baking staples, a small bag of pecan pieces kept in the freezer is always ready for a quick bake.

Roasted, salted and flavoured nuts

Roasting changes the structure of the surface and often makes flavour more delicate. Salted and glazed nuts also attract moisture, which can leave them tacky or soft.

  • Cool roasted nuts completely before sealing them.
  • Keep flavoured nuts in airtight containers and eat them first.
  • If glazed or sugary nuts turn sticky, store them with a sheet of baking parchment between layers.

For the home-roasting side of things, see how to roast almonds at home.

How to tell if nuts have gone off

Trust your nose and your teeth.

  1. Smell: fresh nuts smell sweet or neutral. Stale ones smell sharp, sour, soapy or like old crayons or paint.
  2. Taste: a bitter, harsh or metallic taste means the oils have turned. Spit it out and discard the batch.
  3. Texture: soft, rubbery or limp nuts have absorbed moisture. This is not harmful but they will taste dull.
  4. Appearance: discard any nuts with mould, dark spots or a damp, musty smell.

If in doubt, throw them out. The science behind this is explained in why nuts go rancid, and the general term is rancidification.

Buying with storage in mind

A few habits make life easier:

  • Buy smaller amounts of oily nuts, more often.
  • Pick sealed, well-packed bags over loose scoops where you can.
  • Avoid stocking up on nuts you use only in occasional recipes.
  • Rotate your stock so the oldest is used first.

A last word

A jar, a cool cupboard and a bit of fridge space will keep most nuts tasting good for months. Add a date label and a quick sniff before you bake, and wasted nuts will become a thing of the past. Your next batch of banana bread will thank you.

title: Where cashews come from: a plain explainer
description: A plain explainer on how cashews grow, why the shell needs careful handling, and what happens between the tree and the bag you open at home.
html:
Cashews are one of the odd ones. Pick one up and it looks like a plain, curved, creamy snack. But they grow in an unusual way, need more processing than most nuts, and belong to a family that includes some surprising relatives. Here is how a cashew gets from tree to jar, in plain terms.

The tree and the apple

The cashew tree is a tropical evergreen. It thrives in warm, frost-free climates, and it is grown in many parts of the world's tropical belt. You can read a general overview on the cashew page on Wikipedia.

The odd part is the fruit. What looks like the fruit, a fleshy, pear-shaped, yellow or red body, is called the cashew apple. It is a swollen stalk, not a true fruit. The real fruit is the grey-green, kidney-shaped shell that hangs off the bottom of it. Inside that shell sits a single seed: the cashew we eat.

The cashew apple is edible, juicy and rather astringent, and is used locally for drinks and preserves. It bruises easily and does not travel well, so you rarely see it outside growing regions.

Why you never see them in the shell

If you have shopped for almonds or pecans, you may have noticed that you can buy them in the shell. Cashews are almost never sold that way, and there is a good reason.

Between the outer shell and the seed is a layer containing a caustic oil. It can irritate skin, and it is related to the irritants found in some well-known plants. Because of this, cashews cannot simply be cracked open like a walnut. They need careful handling and a processing step to deal with the shell safely.

So the cashew you buy has already been shelled, dealt with and peeled. This extra work is part of why cashews often cost more than some other nuts.

From tree to bag

The path varies from place to place, but the general steps look like this:

  1. Harvesting. Nuts are collected once they have fallen or been picked from the tree. The apple is separated from the shell.
  2. Drying. The shells are dried in the sun so that they are easier to handle and store.
  3. Treating the shell. Heat, such as steaming or roasting, softens the shell and deals with the oil inside it.
  4. Shelling. The shell is cracked open, by hand or by machine, to release the kernel. It is fiddly work, because the kernel is delicate and breaks easily.
  5. Peeling. A thin skin around the kernel is removed after drying.
  6. Grading. Kernels are sorted by size and whether they are whole or broken. Whole pieces are usually more expensive. Broken pieces are perfectly good for sauces, cooking and butters.

Because of the shape and fragility of the kernel, a lot of this still relies on human hands, even where machines help.

Raw cashews are not quite raw

A small surprise: cashews sold as raw have normally been heated during shell processing. That gentle step is part of making them safe to eat. When we say raw cashews, we mean they have not been roasted or flavoured afterward. If you want to understand what roasting adds, see our post on raw vs roasted nuts.

Cashews in the kitchen

Cashews are soft, mildly sweet and rich, which makes them very flexible.

  • Eat them as they come, or choose salted roasted cashews for an easy snack.
  • Go for flavour with chilli lime cashews if you like heat and zing.
  • Blend them into a smooth, creamy cashew butter, or make your own with our food processor nut butter guide.
  • Soak and blend raw cashews to make a creamy base for sauces and dairy-free desserts.
  • Toss into stir-fries and curries for crunch and richness.

Are they nuts?

Botanically, the cashew is a seed that grows on the outside of its fruit, so the botanical definition does not match what we mean in the kitchen. In cooking and on the label, though, it is treated as a tree nut. That matters for allergies, covered in our guide to reading food labels.

Storage

Cashews are rich in oil, so keep them in an airtight container away from heat. If they smell sharp or paint-like, they have gone off.

In short

A cashew is a seed hanging beneath a swollen fruit stalk, protected by a shell you do not want to bite. It needs treatment, shelling and peeling before it reaches your bowl. Seen that way, the price makes more sense.

For allergy questions, read the label and speak to a qualified professional.

title: Almond flour vs ground almonds
description: Almond flour and ground almonds look alike but differ in texture and blanching. Learn when to swap them in cakes, macarons and gluten-free baking.
html:
Open three different recipes and you may find three different names for what looks like the same powdery ingredient: almond flour, almond meal, ground almonds. They are close relatives, but not always interchangeable. Knowing the difference can save a cake from turning heavy or a batch of biscuits from spreading into one big sheet.

The short version

Both are simply almonds that have been ground up. The differences come down to three things:

  1. Whether the skins were removed first. Blanched almonds have had their brown skins taken off. Unblanched almonds keep them.
  2. How finely they are milled. A powder can be coarse and sandy or very fine and soft.
  3. What the label calls it. Naming varies by country and by brand, so the words alone do not tell you much.

In general, "almond flour" suggests a finer, paler powder made from blanched almonds, while "ground almonds" or "almond meal" can be slightly coarser and sometimes speckled with skin. But there is no strict rule, so read the packet.

What blanching changes

Blanching removes the thin brown skin. Skinless almonds grind to a pale cream colour with a smooth, even texture. Skin-on almonds give a speckled, slightly darker powder with a touch more bitterness and a rustic look.

  • Blanched: best for pale cakes, delicate sponges, macarons and anything where colour and smoothness matter.
  • Unblanched: fine for brownies, rustic tarts, muffins and anything dark or spiced where the skins disappear.

Our ground almonds are a good everyday choice for sponges and tarts. Always check the product page for details on whether skins are included.

Texture and grind

A fine grind absorbs liquid differently and produces a tender, even crumb. A coarser grind gives a slightly sandy, moister result with more bite.

For most home baking, the difference is small. Where it matters:

  • Macarons and French-style meringues: fine, blanched flour is a must. Coarse particles make the shells bumpy and prevent them from rising smoothly.
  • Cakes and frangipane: either works, though finer will be silkier.
  • Biscuits and cookies: coarse can add pleasant texture.
  • Breading and crusts: coarse is fine, even preferred, for a crunchy coating.

If your almond powder feels damp or clumpy, it may have been overground. Overgrinding releases the oils and starts to turn the powder into a paste, so stop as soon as it looks like fine crumbs.

Making your own

You can grind almonds at home with a food processor, though it takes a little care.

  1. Start with whole raw almonds. If you want blanched flour, blanch them first: pour boiling water over them, leave for 1 minute, drain and slip off the skins. Dry them completely.
  2. Make sure the nuts are fully cool and dry. Warm or damp almonds turn to paste.
  3. Use short pulses, not a continuous run. Pulse for one or two seconds at a time.
  4. Stop when you have a fine, sandy powder. This usually takes 30 to 60 seconds in total.
  5. Sift out any larger pieces and grind them again.

Add a spoonful of sugar or flour from the recipe to the bowl as you grind. The dry ingredient soaks up some of the oil and helps prevent paste. Homemade powder is best used within a few days, or stored in the fridge, since fresh grinds lose flavour quickly. If you ever end up with a paste by accident, congratulations: you have made almond butter. See homemade nut butter in a food processor for how to do that on purpose.

Swapping in recipes

Can you swap one for the other? Usually, yes, with a few caveats.

  • Cakes and tarts: swap freely, though expect small differences in colour and crumb.
  • Macarons: stick to fine, blanched flour.
  • Gluten-free baking: almond powder replaces wheat flour only partly. It has no gluten, so it needs eggs, binders or a flour blend. Follow a recipe designed for it rather than swapping one-for-one in a wheat recipe.
  • Weight vs volume: a cup of almond flour and a cup of ground almonds can weigh slightly different amounts. Weigh by grams if the recipe gives them.

If a recipe lists "almond meal", ground almonds are a safe substitute for most uses.

Don't confuse it with flaked almonds

Flaked almonds are thin slices, not ground powder. They are meant for scattering over bakes, toasting for texture or folding into granola. If you want to see how they fit into everyday recipes, our baking category has the full range.

A note on allergens

Almond powder is a tree nut product. Anyone with a tree nut allergy should avoid it and read every label carefully, since almond flour appears in unexpected places such as gluten-free mixes and some sauces. See nut allergies and reading food labels for general guidance.

Storage

Ground almonds have much more surface area than whole ones, so their oils are exposed to air more readily and they go stale faster. Keep the bag tightly sealed and store it somewhere cool and dark. For longer storage, an airtight container in the fridge helps. You can learn more about the almond itself on its Wikipedia page.

A last word

Check whether your powder is blanched, check how fine it is, and match it to the job. For most cakes, either works. For macarons, go fine and pale. And if the recipe calls for something you do not have, a quick pulse of whole almonds is only a minute away.

title: Maple-glazed pecans at home in 20 minutes
description: Make crisp, shiny maple-glazed pecans on the hob or in the oven. Quantities, temperatures and fixes for sticky, burnt or chewy batches.
html:
Maple-glazed pecans disappear fast. They are crunchy, a little sticky, and somewhere between candy and a proper snack. They are also one of the easier things to make at home, needing four ingredients and about twenty minutes. The hard part is stopping at one handful.

Here are two methods, one on the hob and one in the oven, plus how to rescue a batch that has gone wrong.

Ingredients

Makes about 200 g (2 cups), enough for a snack bowl or a salad topping.

  • 200 g (2 cups) raw pecan halves
  • 3 tablespoons pure maple syrup
  • 1 tablespoon soft brown sugar
  • 1/2 teaspoon fine salt
  • 1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon (optional)
  • 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract (optional)

Real maple syrup tastes better than anything labelled as pancake syrup, and it behaves better too, because it caramelises cleanly.

Method one: the oven

This one is hands-off and gives a gentle, even finish.

  1. Heat the oven to 165C (325F). Line a baking tray with baking paper.
  2. Toss the pecans with the syrup, sugar, salt and cinnamon in a bowl until every nut is coated.
  3. Spread in a single layer, with a little space between each nut.
  4. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once halfway, until the glaze is bubbling and the pecans smell toasty.
  5. Remove from the oven. The glaze will look wet. It hardens as it cools.
  6. Leave to cool for 20 minutes, undisturbed, then break apart any clumps.

Method two: the frying pan

This is quicker and gives you a thicker, candy-like coating, but it needs your attention.

  1. Toast the pecans in a dry, heavy frying pan over a medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until you can smell them.
  2. Add the maple syrup and sugar. Stir constantly for 1 to 2 minutes, until the syrup thickens and clings to the nuts.
  3. Take the pan off the heat, sprinkle with salt, and stir in the vanilla.
  4. Tip onto a sheet of baking paper right away and separate the nuts with two forks before they set.

Do not leave the pan, not even for a second. Sugar goes from amber to burnt in about fifteen seconds.

Fixing common problems

They are sticky after cooling

The glaze needs more time or more heat. Return them to a 150C (300F) oven for 5 minutes, then cool again.

They taste burnt

The temperature was too high, or the sugar caught on the tray. Next time, lower the heat and use parchment. Pecans are rich in oil and brown fast, so the line between toasted and bitter is thin.

They went chewy

Humidity is the usual cause. Cool them completely before storing, and keep them in an airtight jar.

The coating is thin

Use a little more syrup, and make sure the nuts are dry and room temperature before you coat them.

Ways to use them

  • Scatter over a salad with soft cheese and bitter leaves.
  • Chop and fold into porridge, yoghurt or ice cream.
  • Use as the topping on pecan pie bars for a sweeter crunch.
  • Pack into small jars as a gift. Our post on building a nut gift box has ideas for the rest of the parcel.
  • Crush them over roasted squash or carrots for a sweet-and-salty edge.

Prefer to buy them?

If you would rather skip the stirring, the catalogue has ready-made maple-glazed pecans. For cooking and baking where the coating is not needed, pecan pieces are a practical shape.

Storing

Cooled, they keep in an airtight container for about a week at room temperature. Beyond that they lose snap. Because pecans contain a lot of natural oil, they can turn stale over time, and the explanation is in why nuts go rancid. If you want to read more about the nut, the pecan page on Wikipedia is a decent overview.

One last word

Pecans are tree nuts. Say so when you share them, check labels on all your ingredients, and ask a qualified professional about any medical question. Otherwise, make a double batch. A single one will not survive the afternoon.

title: Raw vs roasted nuts and what actually changes
description: Compare raw and roasted nuts on flavour, texture, shelf life and cooking, and learn when each one is the better choice for snacks, baking and butters.
html:
Walk down any nut aisle and you will meet the same choice over and over: raw or roasted. It looks like a simple label, but the two behave quite differently in the kitchen. They taste different, crunch differently, keep differently and suit different jobs. Here is a plain look at what roasting actually does, and how to decide which one belongs in your basket.

What "raw" means

A raw nut has been shelled and dried but not cooked to a roasting temperature. It tends to be pale, a little soft and gentle in flavour. Raw nuts taste mild, sometimes slightly green or milky, with a sweetness that sits quietly in the background.

You can eat raw nuts as they are. Many people do. But they are also a starting point: a blank canvas for toasting, seasoning, grinding or soaking.

What roasting does

Heat changes nuts in a few ways.

  • Flavour deepens. Browning reactions create new aroma compounds, giving that warm, toasty, almost caramel note. The Maillard reaction is the name for this kind of browning, and it is the same chemistry that makes toast and seared meat taste so good.
  • Texture crisps. Roasting drives out a little moisture, so nuts snap rather than bend.
  • Colour darkens. From ivory to gold to brown, depending on how far you push it.
  • Aroma intensifies. Roasted nuts smell much stronger, which is a big part of why they taste more flavourful.

Roasting does not magically make nuts sweeter. It makes them taste more of themselves.

Dry roasted, oil roasted, flavoured

Not all roasted nuts are made the same way.

  • Dry roasted: heated without added oil. The flavour is clean and nutty. Our dry-roasted almonds are an example.
  • Oil roasted: cooked in a little oil, which can make the surface richer and glossier.
  • Salted or flavoured: seasoning is added before or after roasting. The salted roasted cashews are a good illustration of how a little salt lifts a mild nut.

Check the ingredients if you care about added oil, salt or sugar. A pack that says "roasted" does not tell you which method was used.

Side-by-side comparison

Raw Roasted
Flavour Mild, milky, sweet Toasty, rich, stronger
Texture Firm to slightly soft Crisp, snappy
Aroma Faint Strong
Best for Baking, butters, soaking, home roasting Snacking, toppings, trail mixes
Keeping Longer in a cool, dark place Shorter, since flavour fades faster

The shelf-life point is worth noting. Roasted nuts have exposed, heat-treated surfaces and tend to lose their freshness sooner. For the details, read why nuts go rancid.

When to choose raw

Raw nuts are the better pick when you plan to do something else with them.

  1. Baking. Nuts bake in the oven anyway, so starting raw avoids over-toasting. A cake with raw almonds on top will brown nicely while it bakes.
  2. Making nut butter. Raw nuts can be roasted at home to the exact depth you want before blending.
  3. Home roasting. You control the colour and the seasoning. Try the method in how to roast almonds at home.
  4. Soaking and milks. Softer raw nuts blend more smoothly into creamy drinks and sauces.
  5. Long storage. If you will not eat them soon, raw nuts usually keep longer.

Raw cashews are a good example. They are soft, mild and creamy, which is exactly why they blend so well into sauces and desserts.

When to choose roasted

Roasted nuts win when you want flavour and crunch straight from the jar.

  1. Snacking. The aroma and snap are the point.
  2. Toppings. A handful of roasted nuts over salad, porridge or ice cream adds instant contrast.
  3. Trail mixes. Roasted nuts hold their crunch against dried fruit better than soft raw ones. See a guide to building a trail mix for how to combine them.
  4. Seasoned snacks. Salt, spices and glazes cling better to warm, roasted surfaces.

A word on "healthier"

It is tempting to say one type is better for you. We do not make claims like that here. Both are nuts, both are eaten in the same way, and the practical differences are about taste, texture and what you want to cook. If you have specific dietary questions, a registered dietitian is the right person to ask.

Can you roast raw nuts later?

Yes, and often it is a good idea. If you buy raw nuts and find they have gone slightly soft in a humid kitchen, a few minutes in a warm oven brings them back to life. Spread them on a tray at 150C (300F) for 5 to 8 minutes, then cool them completely. Roasted nuts cannot be un-roasted, so raw gives you more flexibility.

A last word

If you cook a lot, keep raw nuts in the cupboard and roast small batches when you need them. If you snack a lot, keep a jar of roasted ones nearby and replace it often. Either way, you cannot go far wrong, and the difference between them is a good excuse to try both side by side.

title: Homemade granola with nuts and big clusters
description: Bake nutty granola with proper clusters at home. Ratios, oven temperatures, timings and the one trick for crunch that lasts all week.
html:
Shop granola is fine. Homemade granola is a different thing: warm from the oven, thick with clusters, and as nutty or as light on sugar as you like. It also takes about ten minutes of effort and an hour of walking past the oven and sniffing. This recipe gives you big, crunchy clumps and a jar that stays crisp, with a few swaps for different tastes.

The basic ratio

Granola follows a simple formula, and once you know it you can improvise forever.

  • 3 parts rolled oats
  • 1 part nuts and seeds
  • A little under 1/2 part sweetener and fat combined, roughly equal quantities of each
  • Salt and spice to taste

The wet part binds everything together and caramelises as it bakes. Too much and the granola goes sticky, too little and it will not clump.

Ingredients

Makes about 700 g (a large jar).

  • 300 g (3 cups) old-fashioned rolled oats
  • 150 g (1 cup) mixed nuts, such as raw almonds, raw hazelnuts and chopped walnuts
  • 2 tablespoons sesame or pumpkin seeds (optional)
  • 80 ml (1/3 cup) maple syrup or honey
  • 60 ml (1/4 cup) neutral oil or melted coconut oil
  • 1 egg white
  • 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
  • 1/2 teaspoon fine salt
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  • 60 g (1/2 cup) dried fruit, added after baking

Prepare the nuts

Chop the almonds and hazelnuts roughly, so each piece is about the size of a chickpea or a little larger. Large whole nuts are lovely, but they fall out of clusters and are a bit hard on teeth. The walnuts are already small. If you want the hazelnuts to taste their best, our guide on toasting and skinning hazelnuts shows how, though for granola the oven does that work for you.

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 150C (300F). Line a large baking tray with baking paper.
  2. In a big bowl, mix the oats, nuts, seeds, cinnamon and salt.
  3. In a small jug, whisk the syrup, oil and vanilla.
  4. Pour the wet mixture over the dry and stir until everything is evenly coated and glistening.
  5. In a clean bowl, whisk the egg white until frothy, then stir it through. This is the secret to clusters: the white dries into a crisp glue.
  6. Tip onto the tray and spread in a layer about 2 cm (3/4 inch) thick. Press it down firmly with the back of a spatula.
  7. Bake for 20 minutes. Rotate the tray, but do not stir.
  8. Bake for another 10 to 15 minutes, until deep golden and fragrant. The granola will still feel soft. It crisps up as it cools.
  9. Leave it completely undisturbed for 45 minutes, so the sheet sets as one slab.
  10. Break it into chunks of whatever size you like, and stir through the dried fruit.

Getting the crunch right

Do not stir while it bakes

Stirring breaks up the forming clusters. Rotating the tray gives even colour without disturbing the layer.

Press and wait

Pressing compacts the mixture, and cooling lets the sugar harden. Break it only when it is truly cold.

Add fruit at the end

Dried fruit baked with the granola turns into rock-hard, burnt pebbles. Stir it in after.

Mind the nuts

Nuts burn long before oats do, especially smaller chopped pieces. If your oven runs hot, turn the temperature down to 140C (275F) and bake a little longer.

Variations

  • Replace half the oats with puffed grains or coconut flakes.
  • The granola article on Wikipedia is a good starting point for the history and variety of this breakfast staple.
  • Stir in a spoonful of homemade nut butter with the wet mix for richer clusters. Our food processor nut butter recipe makes enough for that and some toast.
  • Add orange zest and cardamom in autumn, or ginger and dried apricot for something sunnier.
  • For a no-bake shortcut, a bag of breakfast crunch mix over yoghurt scratches the same itch.

Storage

Cool it fully, then pack into an airtight jar. It keeps well for two to three weeks at room temperature. The nuts will be the first thing to turn stale, so keep the jar out of heat and light. If you have questions about why, how to store nuts covers it.

Serving ideas

Spoon it over yoghurt with fruit, eat it dry from the jar, or crumble it over baked fruit for a quick crumble topping. As granola contains nuts and often seeds, read labels on every ingredient you add if you are cooking for someone with an allergy, and ask a qualified professional about medical concerns.

Now go and enjoy the smell. It lasts about as long as the baking does.

title: Nut allergies and reading food labels
description: General guidance on reading nut and peanut allergen labels, including what to look for, how advisory statements work and when to ask a professional.
html:
This post is general information about reading food labels. It is not medical advice, and it cannot tell you what is safe for you or anyone you cook for. If you or someone in your care has an allergy, a doctor, allergist or registered dietitian is the right person to ask. What follows is a plain guide to the common features of labels, so that reading one feels less like decoding a puzzle.

Peanuts and tree nuts are different things

People often say "nut allergy" as one phrase, but the plant sources differ. A peanut is a legume, in the same family as peas and lentils. Almonds, cashews, walnuts, pecans, hazelnuts, Brazil nuts and pistachios are tree nuts. Some people are allergic to one, some to several, and some to both groups. Rules and labelling lists treat them as separate categories, which is why you will usually see "peanuts" and "tree nuts" named separately on a label.

If you want more background, the Wikipedia pages on peanut allergy and tree nut allergy give a general overview.

Where to look on a pack

Labels carry allergen information in a few places. Check all of them every time.

  1. The ingredients list. In many countries, the most common allergens must be named clearly, often in bold or in a separate statement.
  2. A "contains" statement. Some packs add a short line, such as "Contains: almonds, cashews", near the ingredients.
  3. Advisory statements. Lines such as "may contain nuts" or "made in a facility that also handles peanuts".
  4. The brand and product name. A product called "almond butter" obviously contains almonds, but a hazelnut spread might be listed under a different name.

Read the full label on every purchase, even for products you have bought before. Recipes and suppliers change, and a familiar pack can be different from the last one.

Understanding advisory statements

"May contain" lines are the confusing part. They usually indicate that a food was made in a place where cross-contact could happen, for example on shared equipment or in the same building. They are voluntary in many places, so the absence of one does not guarantee a food is free from traces.

Because wording varies, it helps to remember:

  • "May contain" and "made in a facility that handles" are both warnings about possible cross-contact.
  • The strength of the warning is not always standardised, so you cannot assume one phrase means more or less risk than another.
  • If a statement is unclear, contact the manufacturer or ask a professional how to interpret it for your situation.

Names that hide nuts

Nuts sometimes appear under names you might not expect. Common examples of things worth checking include:

  • Nut pastes and marzipan, which are often made with almonds
  • Nut oils and nut flours, including products labelled as almond flour or ground almonds
  • Praline and nougat
  • Nut-based milks, spreads and butters
  • Granola, trail mixes and baked goods that use nuts as a topping or filling

Our own catalogue is a useful example of how widely nuts appear. A classic trail mix lists several nut types, and a jar of smooth peanut butter contains peanuts as its main ingredient. Single-ingredient products like raw almonds are simple, but anyone with an allergy still needs to read the label and consider cross-contact.

Cross-contact at home

Labels are only part of the picture. In your own kitchen:

  • Wash boards, knives and bowls thoroughly with hot, soapy water after using nuts.
  • Store nuts in sealed, clearly labelled containers, away from other ingredients.
  • Use separate utensils for nut butters and other spreads, so crumbs and residues do not travel.
  • Tell guests and family exactly what is in a dish, and ask them what they need to avoid.

If you bake or cook for others, keep the packaging so you can read out the ingredients when asked. A good habit is to photograph labels before throwing them away.

Eating out and buying loose

Loose nuts, bulk bins and market stalls usually do not come with a full label, and shared scoops can carry traces from one product to another. If you need to avoid a specific allergen, ask the seller about handling and cross-contact before you buy, or choose a sealed, labelled pack instead.

Restaurants and cafes will often have an allergen policy. Ask staff directly rather than guessing from the menu, and mention your allergy clearly each time you order.

Official guidance

Rules for labelling differ between countries, and they change. For authoritative information, go to the source:

  • The US Food and Drug Administration page on food allergies explains how allergens must be declared on packaged food in the United States.
  • The UK Food Standards Agency page on food allergy and intolerance covers the rules and advice for the UK.

When in doubt

If a label is unclear, if an ingredient is unfamiliar, or if you are unsure how a statement applies to you, do not guess. Leave the product on the shelf, contact the manufacturer, and talk to a medical professional. Our FAQ lists the general questions we get about our products, but it cannot replace professional advice either.

A last word

Reading labels carefully, every time, is a habit that takes seconds and can matter a great deal. Keep it routine, keep it boring, and when something does not add up, ask a professional rather than relying on a blog post, including this one. For some context on how nuts differ in the kitchen, you may also like are peanuts really nuts.

title: Walnut banana bread that stays moist
description: A reliable banana bread with toasted walnuts. Ripe banana ratios, mixing tips, bake times and a few swaps so the loaf stays tender for days.
html:
Banana bread has a reputation for being easy, and it is. It also has a reputation for being dry in the middle, gummy on the bottom or flat on top, and those happen to people who think it is too easy to need a recipe. This version leans on very ripe fruit, a gentle hand with the mixing bowl, and a generous handful of toasted walnuts that add crunch and a faint bitterness against the sweetness.

Ingredients

Makes one 900 g (2 lb) loaf, about 10 slices.

  • 3 large, very ripe bananas (about 350 g or 12 oz peeled)
  • 90 g (6 tablespoons) butter, melted and cooled slightly
  • 120 g (generous 1/2 cup) soft light brown sugar
  • 1 egg
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  • 190 g (1 1/2 cups) plain flour
  • 1 teaspoon baking powder
  • 1/2 teaspoon bicarbonate of soda
  • 1/2 teaspoon fine salt
  • 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
  • 100 g (1 cup) chopped walnuts, plus a few extra for the top

Choose the right bananas

Skin should be speckled or mostly brown, and the fruit should feel soft. Underripe bananas taste starchy and add little sweetness. If yours are still yellow, bake them whole on a tray, skins on, at 150C (300F) for 15 minutes. They will turn black and sticky, which is exactly what you want. Cool them before mashing.

Toast the walnuts

Walnuts are the star here, so give them a minute. Spread them on a tray and bake at 175C (350F) for 6 to 8 minutes, until they smell warm and slightly toasty. Walnuts contain a lot of oil and can turn bitter if overdone, so stay close. Starting with raw walnut halves and chopping them yourself gives you bigger, more interesting pieces.

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 175C (350F). Grease a 900 g loaf tin and line it with baking paper.
  2. Mash the bananas in a large bowl with a fork. Some small lumps are fine.
  3. Stir in the melted butter, sugar, egg and vanilla until combined.
  4. In a second bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, salt and cinnamon.
  5. Tip the dry mix into the wet and fold gently, just until you can no longer see flour. Overmixing builds gluten and gives a tough, rubbery crumb.
  6. Fold in the walnuts. Scrape into the tin and scatter the extra walnuts over the top.
  7. Bake for 55 to 65 minutes. A skewer pushed into the centre should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. If the top browns too fast, tent it with foil after 35 minutes.
  8. Cool in the tin for 15 minutes, then lift out onto a rack. Wait at least an hour before slicing, because the crumb needs time to set.

Why it stays moist

  • Melted butter coats the flour and keeps the crumb tender.
  • Sugar holds on to moisture, so do not cut it by more than a spoonful or two.
  • The bananas supply moisture and sweetness. Measure them rather than guessing.
  • Resting it, wrapped, for a day improves the texture noticeably.

Swaps and additions

  • Pecans work well in place of walnuts. Raw pecan halves toast in the same time. If you want a recipe that puts them front and centre, try our pecan pie bars.
  • Add 80 g of dark chocolate chunks for a richer loaf.
  • Replace a quarter of the flour with wholemeal for a nuttier, denser result.
  • A tablespoon of yoghurt or soured milk gives a slightly softer crumb.
  • Swirl in a spoonful of peanut or almond butter before baking, if you have some homemade. Our post on making nut butter in a food processor shows how.

Storing and freezing

Wrap the cooled loaf in baking paper and foil, or keep it in an airtight container, for up to 3 days at room temperature. Slices freeze well: wrap each one individually and toast from frozen for a quick breakfast. Walnuts can go stale in storage, so if you keep a bag open for a long time, check how it smells before using it. The walnut page on Wikipedia has more on the tree and the nut itself.

A note on allergies

Walnuts are tree nuts. If you share your loaf, say so, and always read the labels on every ingredient you use. For medical questions, speak to a qualified professional.

The short version

Ripe bananas, a light hand, toasted walnuts, and patience at the cooling stage. That is all it takes to get a loaf worth slicing a second time.

title: A guide to building a trail mix
description: A practical guide to building your own trail mix, covering ratios, texture balance, flavour pairings and how to keep it crunchy on a long walk.
html:
A good trail mix is a small act of engineering. It should be crunchy and chewy in turns, a little sweet and a little salty, and sturdy enough to survive a rucksack. A bad one is a bag of raisins with a few sad peanuts hiding at the bottom. The difference is mostly down to balance, and balance is easy once you know the rules of thumb.

Start with a ratio

A reliable starting point is the 2:1:1 rule, measured by volume.

  • Two parts nuts and seeds: the backbone of the mix
  • One part dried fruit: for sweetness and chew
  • One part extras: chocolate, coconut, crunchy cereal or something savoury

For a mix that fills one large jar, that might be two cups of nuts, a cup of fruit and a cup of extras. Scale it up or down as you like. If you prefer something more savoury, shrink the fruit and extras to a half part each.

Choose your nuts

Nuts do the heavy lifting, so give them some thought. Variety in size, shape and texture is what makes handfuls interesting.

  • Almonds: firm, reliable and a little sweet. Raw almonds work, and roasted ones add depth.
  • Cashews: buttery and soft-crunchy. Raw cashews bring a gentle sweetness that suits fruit.
  • Peanuts: technically a legume, but they behave like a nut and keep the budget friendly.
  • Walnuts and pecans: richer and slightly bitter, so use them in smaller amounts.
  • Seeds: pumpkin and sunflower seeds add crunch and colour without competing for attention.

Aim for at least three kinds. Two nuts and a seed is a perfectly good start.

Add dried fruit with care

Fruit adds sweetness and a chewy contrast, but too much turns the mix sticky and heavy.

  • Raisins and sultanas are the traditional choice and almost impossible to get wrong.
  • Chopped dates or apricots add a deeper, jammier sweetness. Cut them into pea-sized pieces so they spread through the mix.
  • Dried cranberries or cherries give a tart note.
  • Banana chips and mango strips suit a tropical mix.

Large pieces of fruit can clump together, so chop them or toss them in a spoonful of the other ingredients before mixing.

Pick your extras

The extras are where you give the mix its personality.

  • Chocolate: chips or small chunks. In warm weather they melt, so use dark chocolate or plan to eat the mix in a cool place.
  • Coconut: toasted flakes add lightness.
  • Crunchy cereal or pretzels: these add salt and a different kind of crunch.
  • Spices: a pinch of cinnamon or chilli on the nuts changes the whole character.

If you want a ready-made example of how these elements fit together, our classic trail mix and chocolate orchard mix are good reference points. Browse the whole range in trail mixes.

Balance sweet, salty and crunchy

Taste is a three-way tug of war. A few tips:

  1. Salt is your friend. A mix with no salt tastes flat. Use salted nuts, or toss the nuts with a pinch while warm.
  2. Pair sweet with savoury. Chocolate and salted almonds, or dried mango and chilli cashews, are classic contrasts.
  3. Mix textures. If every ingredient is hard, you are chewing a bag of gravel. Add something soft, something crisp, something chewy.
  4. Keep pieces roughly the same size. Otherwise the heavy bits sink to the bottom and you end up with a layer of raisins.

Three starting recipes

The everyday mix: 2 cups almonds, 1 cup raisins, 1/2 cup dark chocolate chips, 1/2 cup pumpkin seeds.

The tropical mix: 1 cup cashews, 1 cup banana chips, 1/2 cup toasted coconut, 1/2 cup chopped dried mango, 1/2 cup macadamia or peanuts.

The savoury kick: 2 cups mixed roasted nuts, 1 cup pretzel pieces, 1/2 cup sunflower seeds, 1 teaspoon smoked paprika and a pinch of salt.

Toast first for more flavour

A few minutes in the oven wakes up the nuts. Spread them on a tray and roast at 160C (320F) for 8 to 12 minutes, stirring once. Cool them completely before mixing them with fruit or chocolate. Our guide on how to roast almonds at home gives the details.

Keep it crunchy

Moisture is the enemy. Dried fruit holds water and nuts absorb it, so a mix stored for a long time can turn soft and slightly chewy. To slow that:

  • Use an airtight container, and fill it as full as you can so there is little air.
  • Keep it out of heat and sunlight.
  • Make smaller batches more often.
  • For long walks, carry the mix in a sealed bag rather than loose in a pocket.

Chocolate and fruit also affect keeping times, which is another reason to make small batches. For more on how nuts hold up in storage, see storing nuts so they stay fresh.

A note on allergies

Mixes combine many ingredients, so anyone with an allergy should read the label on every component. If you are making a mix to share, tell people exactly what is in it. For general guidance, see the FDA page on food allergies.

A last word

Pick three nuts, one fruit, one extra and a pinch of salt. Taste, adjust, and make a note of what worked. Within a couple of batches you will have a signature mix that no shop-bought bag quite matches, and a few good reasons to go for a walk.

title: Pecan pie bars with a shortbread base
description: A tray bake version of pecan pie: buttery shortbread, a sticky caramel filling and toasted pecans. Easy to slice, easy to share, no fussy pastry.
html:
Pecan pie is wonderful and also a bit of a faff. You need a pastry case, a blind bake, a filling that sets just right, and a very patient guest list. Pecan pie bars keep everything that makes the pie good, the sticky caramel centre, the toasty nuts, the buttery base, and swap the pastry for a simple shortbread you press into a tin. They slice cleanly and travel well.

Ingredients

Makes 16 bars in a 20 cm (8 inch) square tin.

For the base:

  • 150 g (1 cup plus 2 tablespoons) plain flour
  • 40 g (1/3 cup) icing sugar
  • 1/4 teaspoon fine salt
  • 100 g (7 tablespoons) cold butter, cubed

For the filling:

  • 150 g (1 1/2 cups) raw pecan halves
  • 60 g (4 tablespoons) butter
  • 100 g (1/2 cup) soft dark brown sugar
  • 90 g (1/4 cup) golden syrup or maple syrup
  • 2 tablespoons double cream
  • 2 eggs, lightly beaten
  • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  • 1/4 teaspoon fine salt

Toast the pecans first

Raw pecans taste fine, but a few minutes in the oven makes them taste like pecans at their best. Spread them on a tray and bake at 175C (350F) for 7 to 8 minutes, until you can smell them. Watch closely, because they go from golden to bitter quickly. Let them cool, then chop about two thirds roughly and leave the rest whole for the top. If you are short on time, pecan pieces save you the chopping.

Make the base

  1. Line the tin with baking paper, leaving a little overhang on two sides for lifting.
  2. Rub the flour, icing sugar, salt and cold butter together with your fingertips, or pulse in a food processor, until it looks like damp sand.
  3. Tip it into the tin and press firmly into an even layer, using the back of a spoon or the bottom of a measuring cup.
  4. Prick it all over with a fork and chill for 15 minutes.
  5. Bake at 175C (350F) for 18 to 20 minutes, until pale gold at the edges.

While it bakes, make the filling.

Make the filling

  1. Melt the butter in a saucepan over a medium heat. Stir in the brown sugar and syrup.
  2. Bring to a gentle bubble and cook for 1 minute, stirring, then take off the heat.
  3. Stir in the cream, vanilla and salt. Let it cool for 5 minutes. This matters: hot caramel will scramble the eggs.
  4. Whisk in the eggs until smooth.
  5. Fold in the chopped pecans.

Bake the bars

Pour the filling over the hot base, spreading it evenly, then scatter the whole pecans over the top. Return the tin to the oven and bake for 22 to 25 minutes. The edges should be set and puffed slightly, while the centre will still wobble a touch, like a baked custard. It firms up as it cools.

Cool completely in the tin, at least 2 hours. Chilling for an hour in the fridge makes slicing neater. Lift out with the paper overhang, and use a sharp knife, wiped between cuts, to make 16 squares.

Tips and swaps

  • Salt matters. A pinch of flaky salt on the top, once cool, balances the sweetness.
  • Use maple-glazed pecans for the topping if you want a sweeter, crunchier crown. Skip the extra sweetness elsewhere and keep an eye on the baking time.
  • A spoonful of bourbon or strong coffee in place of the vanilla gives a grown-up note.
  • Walnuts work if pecans are unavailable. Our walnut banana bread post has a few more ideas for them.
  • For the topping idea above, our post on maple-glazed pecans at home shows how to make your own.

Storing the bars

Keep them in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 3 days, or in the fridge for up to a week. Separate layers with baking paper so they do not stick. You can freeze them, wrapped well, for a few weeks. Bring them to room temperature before serving, because cold caramel is quite firm.

If you want to read about the nut itself, the pecan entry on Wikipedia covers its origins and varieties.

Before you serve them

Pecans are a tree nut. If you are baking for guests, tell them what is in the tin, and read the labels on every ingredient you use. Anyone with a medical concern should check with a qualified professional.

Everyone else can cut the biggest square. You earned it.

title: How to toast and skin hazelnuts
description: Toast hazelnuts in the oven and rub off the papery skins with a tea towel, plus a baking soda boil for stubborn nuts and tips for even colour.
html:
Hazelnuts have a thin, papery brown skin that clings like it has a grudge. Left on, it adds a faint bitterness and a dry, dusty texture. Toasting loosens it, and a bit of rubbing does the rest. The same toasting also turns a mild, slightly green raw hazelnut into something rich, buttery and unmistakably hazelnutty. It is one of the best returns on ten minutes in the kitchen.

Start with good nuts

Buy raw hazelnuts if you plan to toast them yourself. They should be plump and uniform in size, and when you crack one the kernel should be creamy white with no dark spots or musty smell. Uniform size matters: small nuts will burn while large ones are still pale.

If your hazelnuts are still in their shells, crack them first. Shelled nuts are what we are working with here.

Toasting in the oven

  1. Heat the oven to 180C (350F), or 160C (320F) fan.
  2. Spread the hazelnuts in one layer on a baking tray.
  3. Toast for 10 to 15 minutes, shaking the tray once or twice.
  4. The nuts are ready when the skins have darkened and begun to split and curl, and the kernels beneath are golden. The smell should be warm and sweet.

Do not judge by the skin colour alone. Break one open: the kernel should be a pale golden tan. If it is still white, give it another two minutes. If it is brown all through, you have gone too far.

Skinning with a tea towel

This is the classic method, and it works well on nuts that have toasted fully.

  1. Tip the hot nuts onto a clean tea towel.
  2. Fold the towel over them and leave to steam for 1 to 2 minutes. The trapped heat loosens the skins further.
  3. Rub the bundle firmly between your hands, or roll the nuts around inside it.
  4. Pick out the nuts and shake off the loose skin. Most will come away cleanly.

Expect a few stubborn ones. A bit of skin left on is perfectly fine for snacking, though it is worth picking off the worst for a smooth sauce or paste. Do this over a sink or outside, because the skin flakes get everywhere.

A note on the towel

Use an old one. The brown skins can mark light fabrics, and the oils from warm nuts will leave a faint shadow. A clean, rough cotton towel gives the best grip.

The baking soda boil

If your toasted nuts are still stubbornly skinned, there is a wet method that works on raw hazelnuts directly.

  1. Bring 500ml (about 2 cups) of water to a boil.
  2. Stir in 2 tablespoons of baking soda. It will foam, so use a large pot.
  3. Add 150g (about a cup) of hazelnuts and boil for 3 minutes.
  4. Drain and rinse under cold water. The skins should slip off between your fingers.
  5. Dry the nuts well and toast them as above for 8 to 10 minutes to restore crispness.

The soda raises the alkalinity of the water, which breaks down the skins. The trade-off is that it adds a step and the nuts must be dried and re-toasted. For most cooks, the tea towel is simpler. The boil earns its place when you have a big batch to prepare for a recipe.

Getting an even colour

Some hazelnuts will always toast faster than others. A few things help:

  • Sort by size before roasting and keep each size on its own tray.
  • Shake the tray at the halfway point so nothing sits against the hot metal.
  • Use a light-coloured tray, or line it with parchment.
  • Let the nuts cool on a separate surface so they do not keep cooking.

If a handful comes out slightly over, do not bin them. Chop them finely and use them in a crumble topping where a little extra depth is welcome.

What to do with them

Toasted and skinned hazelnuts are wonderfully versatile:

  • Blitz them into a paste, then into something like a spread. If you would rather skip the work, our hazelnut cocoa spread is made for toast, pancakes and spoons.
  • Grind them for cakes and biscuits. Hazelnut flour gives bakes a nutty, tender crumb, and the toasting step is already done in many recipes.
  • Chop them and scatter over roasted vegetables, salads or porridge.
  • Pair them with chocolate, coffee, pears or orange.

The principle of toasting to deepen flavour applies across nuts. If you want to compare it with the almond version, see how to roast almonds at home. The two nuts behave differently, but the logic of low and slow, then cool quickly, is the same.

Storing toasted hazelnuts

Cool them completely on a tray before storing. Then keep them in an airtight jar in a cool, dark place. Toasted nuts stay fresh for a shorter time than raw ones, so toast only what you will use within a couple of weeks. For more on why, see why nuts go rancid.

If you want to learn more about the nut itself, the Wikipedia page on the hazelnut covers the plant and its varieties.

A last word

Toast until the skins crack, steam them in a towel, rub, and enjoy. It takes about fifteen minutes from tray to bowl, and the difference in flavour is immediate. Once you have done it, a bag of pre-skinned nuts feels a bit like a missed opportunity, though both have their place on a busy day.

title: Homemade nut butter in a food processor
description: Turn roasted nuts into smooth, spoonable nut butter with a food processor. Quantities, timings and fixes for when the mixture goes stubborn.
html:
Nut butter is one of the more magical things a food processor does. You tip in a heap of dry, crunchy nuts, press the button, and a few minutes later you are scraping a glossy, pourable spread out of the bowl. There is no secret ingredient. The nuts simply release their own oil as the blades break them down, and that oil turns the powder into butter.

This guide covers the method, the timings you can expect, and what to do when things look like they have gone wrong. They almost never have.

What you need

For roughly one standard jar (about 300 g or 10 oz of finished butter):

  • 350 g (12 oz) nuts, such as dry-roasted almonds, roasted hazelnuts or roasted peanuts
  • 1/2 teaspoon fine salt, or to taste
  • 1 to 2 teaspoons neutral oil, only if the butter stays thick
  • Optional: 1 tablespoon maple syrup or honey, a pinch of cinnamon

You also need a food processor with a decent motor and a bowl of at least 1.5 litres. A small chopper will overheat. A high-powered blender can work, but it needs a tamper and patience.

Start with warm, roasted nuts

Roasted nuts make better butter than raw ones. Heat loosens the oils and brings out flavour, so the nuts break down faster and taste deeper. If you are starting with raw cashews or raw almonds, roast them first on a tray at 160C (325F) for 10 to 12 minutes, until fragrant and lightly golden. Our guide on how to roast almonds at home walks through the details.

Let them cool for about five minutes. You want them warm, not hot. Warm nuts blend more easily, while piping hot ones can scorch the motor of a weaker machine.

The method

  1. Tip the warm nuts into the food processor and add the salt.
  2. Run the machine for 1 minute. The nuts will become a coarse crumb.
  3. Scrape down the sides and run for another 1 to 2 minutes. You will get a dry, sandy powder that clumps up into a ball.
  4. Scrape again. Run for 2 to 3 minutes. The ball will collapse into a thick paste as the oil starts to flow.
  5. Keep going for a further 2 to 4 minutes, pausing to scrape every minute or so, until the butter is glossy and smooth.
  6. Taste, then add any sweetener, spice or a teaspoon of oil. Pulse for 20 seconds to mix.

In total, expect 6 to 10 minutes for almonds and peanuts, and somewhere around 8 to 12 for harder nuts. Hazelnuts are generous with their oil and often finish sooner. If the bowl feels hot to the touch, switch off for five minutes and let it rest.

Troubleshooting

It will not turn smooth

Almost always, this is a patience problem. The powder stage looks hopeless and then suddenly it is not. Keep running, and keep scraping. If it still looks stiff after ten minutes, add a teaspoon of neutral oil and run again.

It is gritty

Some nuts, almonds in particular, leave a fine grain even when well processed. Run it a couple of minutes longer, or accept a slightly rustic texture. Plenty of people prefer it.

It is runny

Warm nut butter is thinner than cold. Pour it into a jar and leave it for an hour before judging. If it is still loose, a tablespoon of finely ground nuts stirred in will thicken it.

The oil has separated

That is normal in any butter without added stabilisers. Stir it back in. Storing the jar upside down for a day before you open it helps redistribute things.

Flavour ideas

  • Cinnamon and a spoonful of maple syrup into almond butter
  • A little cocoa powder and sugar into hazelnut butter, which lands somewhere near a hazelnut cocoa spread
  • Flaky salt and a squeeze of honey into peanut butter
  • A pinch of chilli flakes into cashew butter for something savoury

If you want chunks, remove a handful of nuts before the final blend, chop them roughly, and fold them in at the end.

Storing it

Spoon the butter into a clean, dry jar and cool it before sealing. It will keep in a cupboard for a couple of weeks, and longer in the fridge, where it firms up. Homemade butter has no preservatives, so use a clean spoon each time. The reasons fats turn stale are explained in why nuts go rancid, and the same advice applies here.

For background on the spread itself, the nut butter article on Wikipedia is a reasonable starting point.

Not in the mood to make it?

Fair enough. The nut butters category has ready-made jars, and a jar of almond butter is also a handy benchmark for the texture you are aiming for at home.

Whichever way you go, remember to check ingredient lists if anyone eating it has an allergy. Read the label, and ask a qualified professional about medical questions.

title: How to roast almonds at home
description: Roast raw almonds in a home oven or a dry pan, with temperatures, timings and cues for colour and aroma so every batch comes out crisp and even.
html:
A raw almond is pale, firm and a little mild. Roast it for a few minutes and it turns into something else: deeper in colour, louder in aroma, and noticeably crunchier. The good news is that you need nothing more than an oven, a baking tray and a bit of patience. The less good news is that almonds go from perfect to bitter faster than you would expect, so this is a job where you stay in the kitchen.

What you need

Start with raw almonds, whole and with their skins on. Whole almonds roast more evenly than broken ones, and the skin adds a toasty, slightly tannic edge. You will also need:

  • A rimmed baking tray, ideally light-coloured, since dark trays run hotter
  • Baking parchment (optional, but it makes cleanup easy)
  • A wooden spoon or spatula
  • A cooling plate or second tray

You do not need oil. Almonds carry plenty of their own fat. For salt or spice, add it after roasting while the nuts are warm.

Roasting in the oven

The oven gives the most even result, particularly for a big batch.

  1. Heat the oven to 160C (320F), or 140C (285F) fan.
  2. Spread the almonds in a single layer on the tray. Crowding steams them instead of roasting them, so use two trays if needed.
  3. Roast for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring or shaking the tray at the halfway point.
  4. Start checking at 10 minutes. You are looking for a light golden-brown centre and a warm, sweet, nutty smell.
  5. Tip the nuts onto a cool tray straight away. If they stay on the hot one, they keep cooking.

To check the colour, snap one almond in half. The inside should be tan or pale gold, not white, and certainly not dark brown. Nuts darken a little more as they cool, so pull them slightly before they look finished.

A lower, slower option

If you are roasting a large amount, 150C (300F) for 18 to 22 minutes is more forgiving. The edges of the tray can colour faster than the middle, so stir every five minutes. Slow roasting gives a more even interior and less risk of scorching.

Roasting in a pan

For a handful, a dry frying pan on the hob is quicker.

  1. Warm a heavy-based pan over medium heat for a minute.
  2. Add the almonds in a single layer.
  3. Shake and stir almost constantly for 4 to 6 minutes.
  4. Watch for tiny toasted spots on the skins and that nutty aroma, then tip them out at once.

The pan method is faster but less even, so some almonds will be darker on one side. For snacking that hardly matters. For baking, where appearance counts, use the oven.

Seasoning ideas

Roasted almonds love a light coating while they are warm and slightly tacky with their own oils.

  • Salted: a fine pinch of flaky or fine salt, tossed through in a bowl.
  • Smoky: a little smoked paprika plus salt. If you want the real thing without the effort, our smoked almonds are already done.
  • Sweet and spiced: a pinch of cinnamon with a spoonful of sugar, stirred through hot nuts.
  • Herby: finely chopped rosemary and a little black pepper.

Season in a bowl rather than on the tray, so the flavour sticks evenly.

Troubleshooting

The almonds taste bitter. They were roasted too long or too hot. Dark brown centres mean the sugars have tipped from toasty to burnt. Start a fresh batch and pull them earlier.

They are soft after cooling. Almonds crisp up as they cool, so give them 15 minutes on a cool surface before judging. If they are still chewy, they likely needed a few more minutes in the oven.

Some are dark, some are pale. Mixed sizes roast at different speeds. Next time, sort the almonds by size, or buy a consistent product such as flaked almonds for toppings, which need only 5 to 8 minutes at the same temperature and a very close eye.

Why roast at home at all?

You can certainly buy dry-roasted almonds ready to eat, and plenty of people do. Home roasting is a small pleasure for a few reasons: you choose the degree of roast, you taste the nuts at their warmest and crispest, and the kitchen smells wonderful for an hour afterwards. If you are weighing up the difference between the two states, our post on raw vs roasted nuts covers flavour and texture in more detail.

Storing your roasted almonds

Let the nuts cool completely before they go anywhere, because trapped warmth makes steam and steam makes soft nuts. Store them in an airtight jar in a cool, dark cupboard. Roasted nuts have a shorter life than raw ones, since heat and exposed surfaces speed up staleness. For the full picture, see storing nuts so they stay fresh. A batch made on Sunday should be at its best for the week ahead, and it rarely lasts that long anyway.

For some background on the nut itself, the Wikipedia entry on the almond is a decent starting point.

A last word

Roasting almonds is mostly about attention. Set a timer for the earliest check, trust your nose, and tip the nuts out a minute before you think they are done. Do that, and you will have a jar of crisp, golden almonds that taste far better than they have any right to for the effort involved.
